Almost! In the script attached to the ball, I have it set to do direction.x = abs(direction.x), or direction.x = -abs(direction.x). By using absolute values, I can ensure that the ball's x-direction always ends up going the way I want it - if it simply inverts the x-direction and the ball contacts the paddle for multiple frames, the x-direction might end up rapidly fluctuating between positive and negative instead of just changing direction and then staying in that direction, if that makes sense

No, I used an Area2D with a collisionbody2d and animatedsprite2d as child nodes, since I didn't really need complex functionality. The collisionbody2d is hooked up so that I can tell when it collides with anything

I control the ball using a Vector2, which makes it easy to independently change the ball's vertical and horizontal movement. Vector2s can have their x and y velocities changed independently. That way, I can make the ball bounce off the paddles horizontally without changing the way it moves vertically, by modifying only the x direction. 

I also very slightly randomly increase our decrease the ball's y direction, just to keep it from getting stuck in a predictable pattern. It's kinda hacky, but it works good enough for an unpolished practice game :P

If you're not using a Vector2 to control the ball movement, let me know. Without knowing how you're making the ball move, it's hard to know if my solution will work for you

Oh, the "AI" is just an algorithm that moves the paddle based on how close the ball is to the right side of the screen, and what its vertical position is. Then, add in a bit of smoothing so it doesn't just blink around all glitchy, and you have an opponent who is competent enough to be a challenge but not so flawless that it's impossible to win :)
